introduction-the-rules-of-the-road.core: A handful of protocols carry almost everything: DHCP gives a host its identity (IP, gateway, DNS), ARP maps IPs to MAC addresses on the local link, ICMP reports errors and diagnostics, and TCP and UDP carry application data with or without reliability guarantees. Knowing how each works explains most everyday failures, from 'no IP address' to 'connection reset'.

first_principles.problem: A new VM boots but can't reach anything, and the team doesn't know whether DHCP, ARP or routing is at fault.
truths: Hosts need configuration to join a network.
Data delivery needs a transport choice.

analogy.title: Moving into a new town
analogy.story: Register for an address (DHCP), learn your neighbours' doors (ARP), follow road signs and warnings (ICMP), choose courier or postcard (TCP/UDP).
analogy.breaks: Towns don't expire your address; DHCP leases do.

example.title: Boot sequence

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Each step is a debugging checkpoint.

example.outcome: the protocol journey of a new host.

check.q: Which protocol lets a host find the MAC of its default gateway?

dhcp-getting-an-identity.core: DHCP hands out IP configuration in four steps (DORA): the client broadcasts Discover, servers Offer an address, the client Requests one, and the server Acknowledges with a lease (IP, mask, gateway, DNS, lease time). Clients renew at half the lease time. Relays forward broadcasts across subnets, and rogue DHCP servers or exhausted pools are classic failure modes.

first_principles.problem: Laptops get 169.254.x.x addresses because the DHCP pool on the guest VLAN is exhausted.
truths: New hosts know nothing about the network.
derivation: Size **pools and lease times** for churn.

analogy.title: A hotel front desk
analogy.story: You arrive, ask for a room, are offered one, accept, and get a key valid until checkout, which you can extend.
analogy.breaks: Hotels don't broadcast to find guests; DHCP clients broadcast to find servers.

code.text:
sudo tcpdump -ni eth0 port 67 or port 68 -vv
# DHCP-Discover, DHCP-Offer 10.0.1.15, DHCP-Request, DHCP-ACK lease 86400
sudo dhclient -r eth0 && sudo dhclient -v eth0

check.q: What does a 169.254.x.x address on a client indicate?
check.a: It failed to get a DHCP lease and self-assigned a link-local (APIPA) address.

arp-the-bridge-between-software-and-hard.core: IP addresses are logical, but Ethernet delivers frames to MAC addresses. ARP bridges the two: a host broadcasts 'who has 10.0.1.1?', the owner replies with its MAC, and the answer is cached in the ARP table for a while. Gratuitous ARP announces changes, for example during failover. Because ARP has no authentication, it enables spoofing and man-in-the-middle attacks on local networks.

first_principles.problem: After a VIP fails over to a new server, clients keep sending to the old MAC until their ARP caches expire.

analogy.title: Shouting 'who is Alex?' in an office
analogy.story: Alex answers and you note their desk; if Alex moves desks, they announce it to everyone.
analogy.breaks: Imposters in an office are noticed; ARP spoofers aren't.

code.text:
ip neigh show
# 10.0.1.1 dev eth0 lladdr 0a:1b:2c:3d:4e:5f REACHABLE
arping -U -I eth0 10.0.1.50    # send gratuitous ARP after VIP move

check.q: Why is gratuitous ARP used during failover?
check.a: To immediately update neighbours' caches so traffic for the IP goes to the new MAC instead of the old one.

icmp-the-internets-diagnostic-tool.core: ICMP carries control messages: echo request and reply (ping), destination unreachable (with codes for port, host or fragmentation-needed), time exceeded (which traceroute relies on), and redirects. Blocking all ICMP 'for security' breaks Path MTU Discovery, causing black-holed large packets. Allow at least the essential types while rate-limiting.

first_principles.problem: After a firewall blocks all ICMP, HTTPS uploads hang because 'fragmentation needed' messages no longer arrive.
derivation: Allow **type 3 code 4** (frag needed) / ICMPv6 Packet Too Big.

analogy.title: Return-to-sender notices
analogy.story: The post office tells you 'address unknown' or 'too big for this route'; ignore those notices and parcels just vanish.
analogy.breaks: Post notices are rarely forged; ICMP can be abused, hence rate limits.

code.text:
ping -M do -s 1472 example.com   # 1472 + 28 = 1500: works?
ping -M do -s 1400 example.com   # if only smaller works, path MTU < 1500
tracepath example.com            # reports pmtu per hop

check.q: Why is blocking all ICMP harmful?
check.a: It breaks Path MTU Discovery (and IPv6 neighbour discovery), so large packets silently disappear.

tcp-the-three-way-handshake.core: TCP sets up a connection with SYN (client picks an initial sequence number), SYN-ACK (server acknowledges and picks its own), and ACK. Both sides then agree on sequence numbers, window sizes and options (MSS, window scaling, SACK). Teardown uses FIN/ACK in each direction, and the closing side waits in TIME_WAIT. RST aborts immediately: the classic 'connection reset'.

first_principles.problem: A load test fails with 'connection refused' and nobody knows whether the SYN reached the server.
truths: Both sides need synchronised sequence numbers.
The handshake costs one round trip.

analogy.title: A phone call opening
analogy.story: 'Hello, can you hear me?' 'Yes, can you hear me?' 'Yes.' Only then does the conversation start.
analogy.breaks: Calls don't track byte counts; TCP numbers every byte.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Shows whether SYNs leave, return, or get RST.

code.text:
sudo tcpdump -ni eth0 'tcp[tcpflags] & (tcp-syn|tcp-rst) != 0 and port 443'
# Flags [S]  seq 1000  win 64240 options [mss 1460,sackOK,TS,wscale 7]
# Flags [S.] seq 5000 ack 1001
# (then [.] ack)

check.q: What's the difference between 'connection refused' and a timeout?
check.a: Refused means a RST came back (port closed); a timeout means no reply at all, typically a firewall dropping packets.

tcp-advanced-flow-control-and-congestion.core: Flow control protects the receiver: it advertises a receive window, and the sender never has more unacknowledged bytes in flight than that. Congestion control protects the network: the sender keeps a congestion window that grows (slow start, then congestion avoidance) and shrinks on loss or delay signals. Throughput is roughly min(rwnd, cwnd) / RTT, so high-latency links need big windows.

first_principles.problem: A 1 Gbps transatlantic link only achieves 50 Mbps for a single TCP stream.
truths: In-flight data is bounded per RTT.

analogy.title: Water through a pipe with a tap at each end
analogy.story: The receiver's tap (rwnd) and pipe width (cwnd) limit flow; a long pipe needs more water in it to keep flow up.
analogy.breaks: Pipes don't drop water; networks drop packets to signal congestion.

check.q: What's the difference between flow control and congestion control?
check.a: Flow control prevents overwhelming the receiver (rwnd); congestion control prevents overwhelming the network (cwnd).

tcp-vs-udp-the-fundamental-choice.core: TCP gives reliable, ordered streams at the cost of handshake latency, retransmission delays and head-of-line blocking. UDP gives independent, unordered datagrams with no setup, so applications handle loss themselves. Choose TCP for correctness-critical transfers (web, databases, files) and UDP for real-time, loss-tolerant or custom-reliability traffic (DNS, VoIP, games, video, QUIC).

first_principles.problem: A voice app over TCP stutters badly because one lost packet stalls all audio behind it.
truths: Some data is useless if late.
Apps can build their own reliability.

analogy.title: Registered mail vs live radio
analogy.story: Registered mail guarantees delivery but is slow; live radio keeps going even if you miss a word.
analogy.breaks: Radio is one-way; UDP apps can still request retransmits selectively.

points: Match to data's value over time.

check.q: Why does real-time voice usually prefer UDP?
check.a: Late audio is useless, so waiting for retransmissions (TCP head-of-line blocking) is worse than skipping a lost packet.

udp-and-the-future-quic.core: QUIC builds a reliable, encrypted, multiplexed transport on top of UDP, implemented in user space. It combines the transport and TLS 1.3 handshakes (1-RTT, or 0-RTT on resumption), gives each stream independent loss recovery (no head-of-line blocking across streams), and uses connection IDs so connections survive IP changes, such as switching from Wi-Fi to cellular. HTTP/3 runs on QUIC.

first_principles.problem: Mobile users drop connections when moving between Wi-Fi and 4G, and page loads stall on lossy networks.
truths: TCP is in kernels and middleboxes, so it's hard to evolve.
derivation: Run transport over **UDP** in user space.

analogy.title: A courier service that runs its own vans on public roads
analogy.story: It doesn't wait for road authorities to change rules; it tracks each parcel separately and keeps deliveries going if you move house.
analogy.breaks: Couriers can't be blocked by road type; some networks still block or throttle UDP 443.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Server advertises h3 via Alt-Svc; client upgrades.

code.text:
curl -sI --http3 https://cloudflare.com | head -1
# HTTP/3 200
curl -sI https://cloudflare.com | grep -i alt-svc
# alt-svc: h3=":443"; ma=86400

check.q: How does QUIC avoid TCP's head-of-line blocking?
check.a: Each stream has independent loss recovery, so a lost packet only delays its own stream, not all others.
